s: “Circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter.” Romans 2:29.

1. It is the sad remark of an excellent man that whoever now preaches the most essential duties of Christianity runs the risk of being regarded, by a great part of his hearers, as “a proclaimer of new doctrines.”

Most people have so lived away the substance of that religion whose profession they still retain, that no sooner are any of those truths put forward which distinguish the Spirit of Christ from the spirit of the world than they cry out, “You are bringing strange things to our ears; we want to know what these things mean”—though he is only preaching to them “Jesus and the resurrection,” with its necessary consequence: If Christ is risen, you ought then to die to the world, and to live wholly to God.

2. This is a hard saying to the natural man, who is alive to the world and dead to God; and one that he will not readily be persuaded to receive as the truth of God, unless it is so qualified in the interpretation as to have neither use nor meaning left.

He “does not receive the” words “of the Spirit of God,” taken in their plain and obvious meaning; “they are foolishness to him; nor” indeed “can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” They can be perceived only by that spiritual sense which in him has never yet been awakened; and for lack of it he must reject, as idle fancies of men, what are both the wisdom and the power of God.

3. That “circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter”—that the distinguishing mark of a true follower of Christ, of one who is in a state of acceptance with God, is not outward circumcision, or baptism, or any other outward form, but a right state of soul, a mind and spirit renewed after the image of him who created it—is one of those important truths that can only be spiritually discerned.
And the Apostle himself hints at this in the next words: “Whose praise is not from men, but from God.”
As if he had said, “Do not expect, whoever you are who thus follow your great Master, that the world, those who do not follow him, will say, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant!’
Know that the circumcision of the heart, the seal of your calling, is foolishness to the world.
Be content to wait for your applause until the day of your Lord’s appearing.
On that day you shall have praise from God, in the great assembly of men and angels.”
I intend, first, to inquire in particular what this circumcision of the heart consists of; and, second, to mention some reflections that naturally arise from such an inquiry.
I. 1. I am, first, to inquire what that circumcision of the heart consists of which will receive the praise of God.

In general we may observe that it is that habitual disposition of soul which in the sacred writings is called holiness; and which directly implies being cleansed from sin, “from all filthiness both of flesh and spirit”; and, as a consequence, being endowed with those virtues which were also in Christ Jesus; being so “renewed in the spirit of our mind” as to be “perfect as our Father in heaven is perfect.”
2. To be more specific: circumcision of heart implies humility, faith, hope, and charity.

Humility, a right judgment of ourselves, cleanses our minds from those high notions of our own perfection, from that undue opinion of our own abilities and attainments, which are the genuine fruit of a corrupted nature.
This entirely cuts off that vain thought, “I am rich, and wise, and have need of nothing”; and convinces us that we are by nature wretched, and poor, and miserable, and blind, and naked.

It convinces us that in our best state we are, of ourselves, all sin and vanity; that confusion, and ignorance, and error reign over our understanding; that unreasonable, earthly, sensual, devilish passions usurp authority over our will; in a word, that there is no sound part in our soul, that all the foundations of our nature are out of order.

3. At the same time we are convinced that we are not sufficient of ourselves to help ourselves; that without the Spirit of God we can do nothing but add sin to sin; that it is he alone who works in us by his almighty power, either to will or to do that which is good; it being as impossible for us even to think a good thought, without the supernatural assistance of his Spirit, as to create ourselves, or to renew our whole souls in righteousness and true holiness.

4. A sure effect of our having formed this right judgment of the sinfulness and helplessness of our nature is a disregard of that “honor which comes from man,” which is usually paid to some supposed excellence in us.
He who knows himself neither desires nor values the applause which he knows he does not deserve.
It is therefore “a very small thing to him to be judged by man’s judgment.”

He has every reason to think, by comparing what the world has said, either for or against him, with what he feels in his own breast, that the world, as well as the god of this world, was “a liar from the beginning.”

And even as to those who are not of the world: though he would choose, if it were the will of God, that they should regard him as one who desires to be found a faithful steward of his Lord’s goods, if perhaps this might be a means of enabling him to be of more use to his fellow servants, yet as this is the one purpose of his wishing for their approval, so he does not rest on it at all; for he is assured that whatever God wills, he can never lack instruments to carry it out, since he is able, even from these stones, to raise up servants to do his pleasure.
5. This is that lowliness of mind which those who follow his example and tread in his steps have learned from Christ.

And this knowledge of their disease, by which they are more and more cleansed from one part of it, pride and vanity, disposes them to embrace with a willing mind the second thing implied in circumcision of the heart—that faith which alone is able to make them whole, which is the one medicine given under heaven to heal their sickness.
6. The best guide of the blind, the surest light of those who are in darkness, the most perfect instructor of the foolish, is faith.

But it must be such a faith as is “mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds”—to the overturning of all the prejudices of corrupt reason, all the false maxims revered among men, all evil customs and habits, all that “wisdom of the world which is foolishness with God”; such a faith as “casts down imaginations,” reasonings, “and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and brings into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.”
7. “All things are possible to him who” thus “believes.”

“The eyes of his understanding being enlightened,” he sees what his calling is: namely, to glorify God, who has bought him at so high a price, in his body and in his spirit, which are now God’s by redemption as well as by creation.
He feels what is “the exceeding greatness of this power” of him who, as he raised up Christ from the dead, so is able to “make us alive, who are dead in sin, by his Spirit who dwells in us.”

“This is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith”; that faith which is not only an unshaken assent to all that God has revealed in Scripture—and in particular to those important truths, “Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners”; “He bore our sins in his own body on the tree”; “He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world”—but likewise the revelation of Christ in our hearts; a divine evidence or conviction of his love, his free, unmerited love to me a sinner; a sure confidence in his pardoning mercy, worked in us by the Holy Spirit; a confidence by which every true believer is enabled to bear witness, “I know that my Redeemer lives,” that I have an “Advocate with the Father,” and that “Jesus Christ the righteous” is my Lord, and “the propitiation for my sins”—I know he has “loved me, and given himself for me”—he has reconciled me, even me, to God; and I “have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.”

8. Such a faith as this cannot fail to show clearly the power of him who inspires it, by delivering his children from the yoke of sin, and “purging their consciences from dead works”; by strengthening them so that they are no longer compelled to obey sin in its desires; but instead of yielding their members to it “as instruments of unrighteousness,” they now “yield themselves” entirely “to God, as those who are alive from the dead.”
9. Those who are thus born of God by faith also have strong consolation through hope.
This is the next thing which the circumcision of the heart implies: namely, the testimony of their own spirit with the Spirit who witnesses in their hearts that they are the children of God.

Indeed, it is the same Spirit who works in them that clear and cheerful confidence that their heart is upright toward God; that good assurance that they now do, through his grace, the things which are acceptable in his sight; that they are now in the path which leads to life, and shall, by the mercy of God, endure in it to the end.
It is he who gives them a lively expectation of receiving all good things at God’s hand; a joyful prospect of that crown of glory which is reserved in heaven for them.
By this anchor a Christian is kept steady in the midst of the waves of this troubled world, and preserved from striking upon either of those fatal rocks—presumption or despair.
He is neither discouraged by a misconceived severity of his Lord, nor does he despise the riches of his goodness.

He neither imagines the difficulties of the race set before him to be greater than he has strength to conquer, nor expects them to be so small as to give way in the conflict before he has put forth all his strength.

The experience he already has in the Christian warfare, as it assures him that his “labor is not in vain” if “whatever his hand finds to do, he does it with his might,” so it forbids him to entertain so vain a thought as that he can gain any advantage in any other way, that any virtue can be shown, any praise attained, by faint hearts and feeble hands; or indeed by any but those who pursue the same course as the great Apostle of the Gentiles: “I,” he says, “so run, not with uncertainty; so I fight, not as one who beats the air. But I keep my body under control and bring it into subjection, lest by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be cast away.”
10. By the same discipline every good soldier of Christ is to train himself to endure hardship.
Confirmed and strengthened by this, he will be able to renounce not only the works of darkness, but every appetite too, and every affection, which is not subject to the law of God.
For “everyone,” says St. John, “who has this hope purifies himself, just as he is pure.”

It is his daily care, by the grace of God in Christ and through the blood of the covenant, to purge the inmost recesses of his soul from the lusts that previously possessed and defiled it; from uncleanness, and envy, and malice, and wrath; from every passion and temper that is after the flesh, that either springs from or nourishes his native corruption; knowing well that he whose very body is the temple of God ought to admit into it nothing common or unclean, and that holiness befits that house forever where the Spirit of holiness is pleased to dwell.
11. Yet you lack one thing, whoever you are, who to a deep humility and a steadfast faith have joined a lively hope, and thereby in good measure cleansed your heart from its inborn pollution.
If you would be perfect, add to all these charity; add love, and you have the circumcision of the heart. “Love is the fulfilling of the law, the end of the commandment.”
Very excellent things are spoken of love; it is the essence, the spirit, the life of all virtue.
It is not only the first and great commandment, but it is all the commandments in one.
“Whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely,” or honorable, “if there is any virtue, if there is any praise,” they are all included in this one word—love.
In this is perfection, and glory, and happiness.
The royal law of heaven and earth is this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.”
12. Not that this forbids us to love anything besides God: it implies that we love our brother also.
Nor does it forbid us (as some have strangely imagined) to take pleasure in anything but God.

To suppose this is to suppose that the Fountain of holiness is directly the author of sin, since he has inseparably joined pleasure to the use of those creatures which are necessary to sustain the life he has given us.
This, therefore, can never be the meaning of his command.
What its real sense is, both our blessed Lord and his apostles tell us too frequently and too plainly to be misunderstood.

They all with one voice bear witness that the true meaning of those several declarations—“The Lord your God is one Lord”; “You shall have no other gods but me”; “You shall love the Lord your God with all your strength”; “You shall cling to him”; “The desire of your soul shall be to his name”—is no other than this: The one perfect Good shall be your one ultimate end.
One thing you shall desire for its own sake—the enjoyment of him who is All in All.
One happiness you shall set before your souls: union with him who made them; having “fellowship with the Father and the Son”; being joined to the Lord in one Spirit.
One purpose you are to pursue to the end of time—the enjoyment of God in time and in eternity.
Desire other things so far as they tend to this.
Love the creature as it leads to the Creator.
But in every step you take, let this be the glorious point that ends your view.
Let every affection, and thought, and word, and work be subordinate to this.
Whatever you desire or fear, whatever you seek or shun, whatever you think, speak, or do, let it be in order to your happiness in God, the sole End as well as Source of your being.
13. Have no end, no ultimate end, but God.
Thus our Lord: “One thing is needful”; and if your eye is singly fixed on this one thing, “your whole body shall be full of light.”
Thus St. Paul: “This one thing I do; I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus.”
Thus St. James: “Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”
Thus St. John: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”

Seeking happiness in what gratifies either the desire of the flesh, by pleasantly striking the outward senses; or the desire of the eye, of the imagination, by its novelty, greatness, or beauty; or the pride of life, whether by pomp, grandeur, power, or their usual consequence, applause and admiration—this “is not of the Father”; it neither comes from, nor is approved by, the Father of spirits; it is “of the world”: it is the distinguishing mark of those who will not have him to reign over them.
II. 1. Thus I have inquired in particular what that circumcision of heart is which will obtain the praise of God.
I am, in the second place, to mention some reflections that naturally arise from such an inquiry, as a plain rule by which every man may judge of himself whether he is of the world or of God.

And, first, it is clear from what has been said that no man has a claim to the praise of God unless his heart is circumcised by humility; unless he is little, and base, and vile in his own eyes; unless he is deeply convinced of that inborn “corruption of his nature,” “by which he is very far gone from original righteousness,” being prone to all evil, averse to all good, corrupt and abominable; having a “carnal mind which is enmity against God, and is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can be”; unless he continually feels in his inmost soul that without the Spirit of God resting upon him he can neither think, nor desire, nor speak, nor do anything good or well-pleasing in his sight.

No man, I say, has a claim to the praise of God until he feels his need of God; nor indeed until he seeks that “honor which comes from God alone,” and neither desires nor pursues that which comes from man, except only so far as it tends to this.

2. Another truth, which naturally follows from what has been said, is that no one shall obtain the honor that comes from God unless his heart is circumcised by faith, even a “faith of the operation of God”: unless, refusing to be led any longer by his senses, appetites, or passions, or even by that blind leader of the blind so idolized by the world, natural reason, he lives and walks by faith; directs every step as one “seeking him who is invisible”; “looks not at the things which are seen, which are temporal, but at the things which are not seen, which are eternal”; and governs all his desires, plans, and thoughts, all his actions and conduct, as one who has entered within the veil, where Jesus sits at the right hand of God.

3. It is to be wished that those were better acquainted with this faith who spend much of their time and effort laying another foundation: grounding religion on the eternal fitness of things, on the intrinsic excellence of virtue and the beauty of actions flowing from it; on the reasons, as they call them, of good and evil, and the relations of beings to each other.
Either these accounts of the grounds of Christian duty agree with the scriptural account, or they do not.
If they do, why are well-meaning people perplexed, and drawn away from the weightier matters of the law, by a cloud of terms, by which the easiest truths are explained into obscurity?

If they do not, then it is fitting for them to consider who is the author of this new doctrine; whether he is likely to be an angel from heaven who preaches another gospel than that of Christ Jesus; though, if he were, God, not we, has pronounced his sentence: “Let him be accursed.”

4. Our gospel, as it knows no other foundation of good works than faith, or of faith than Christ, so it clearly informs us that we are not his disciples while we deny either him to be the Author, or his Spirit to be the Inspirer and Perfecter, of both our faith and our works.
“If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.”

He alone can give life to those who are dead to God, can breathe into them the breath of Christian life, and so go before, accompany, and follow them with his grace as to bring their good desires to good effect.
And “as many as are thus led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.”
This is God’s short and plain account of true religion and virtue; and “other foundation can no one lay.”

5. From what has been said we may, third, learn that no one is truly “led by the Spirit” unless that “Spirit bears witness with his spirit that he is a child of God”; unless he sees the prize and the crown before him, and “rejoices in hope of the glory of God.”
So greatly have they erred who have taught that in serving God we ought not to have a view to our own happiness!

No, but we are often and expressly taught by God to have “respect to the recompense of the reward”; to balance toil with the “joy set before us,” these “light afflictions” with that “exceeding weight of glory.”

Yes, we are “aliens to the covenant of promise,” we are “without God in the world,” until God, “of his abundant mercy, has begotten us again to a living hope of the inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, and that does not fade away.”

6. But if these things are so, it is high time for those persons to deal faithfully with their own souls who are so far from finding in themselves this joyful assurance that they fulfill the terms, and shall obtain the promises, of that covenant, that they quarrel with the covenant itself and blaspheme its terms; complaining that they are too severe, and that no man ever did or shall live up to them.

What is this but to reproach God, as if he were a hard Master, requiring of his servants more than he enables them to perform?—as if he had mocked the helpless works of his hands by binding them to impossibilities; by commanding them to overcome where neither their own strength nor grace was sufficient for them?
7. These blasphemers might almost persuade those to imagine themselves guiltless who, at the opposite extreme, hope to fulfill the commands of God without taking any pains at all.

Vain hope! that a child of Adam should ever expect to see the kingdom of Christ and of God without striving, without agonizing, first “to enter in at the narrow gate”; that one who was “conceived and born in sin,” and whose “inward parts are very wickedness,” should once entertain a thought of being “purified as his Lord is pure,” unless he treads in his steps and “takes up his cross daily”; unless he “cuts off his right hand,” and “plucks out the right eye, and casts it from him”; that he should ever dream of shaking off his old opinions, passions, and tempers, of being “sanctified throughout in spirit, soul, and body,” without a constant and continued course of general self-denial!

8. What less than this can we possibly infer from the above-cited words of St. Paul, who, living “in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses” for Christ’s sake; who, being full of “signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds”; who, having been “caught up into the third heaven,” yet reckoned, as a recent author strongly expresses it, that all his virtues would be insecure, and even his salvation in danger, without this constant self-denial?

“So I run,” he says, “not with uncertainty; so I fight, not as one who beats the air”; by which he plainly teaches us that he who does not thus run, who does not thus deny himself daily, does run uncertainly, and fights to as little purpose as he who “beats the air.”

9. To as little purpose does he talk of “fighting the fight of faith,” and as vainly does he hope to attain the crown of incorruption (as we may, lastly, infer from the preceding observations), whose heart is not circumcised by love.

Love, cutting off both the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life—engaging the whole man, body, soul, and spirit, in the ardent pursuit of that one object—is so essential to a child of God that, without it, whoever lives is counted dead before him.
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and do not have love, I am like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
Though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and do not have love, I am nothing.”
Indeed, “though I give all my goods to feed the poor, and my body to be burned, and do not have love, it profits me nothing.”
10. Here, then, is the sum of the perfect law; this is the true circumcision of the heart.
Let the spirit return to God who gave it, with the whole train of its affections.
“To the place from which all the rivers came, there let them flow again.
Other sacrifices from us he would not have; but the living sacrifice of the heart he has chosen.
Let it be continually offered up to God through Christ, in flames of holy love.
And let no creature be allowed to share with him; for he is a jealous God.
His throne he will not divide with another; he will reign without a rival.
Let no design, no desire be admitted there but what has him for its ultimate object.
This is the way in which those children of God once walked who, being dead, still speak to us.” “Desire not to live but to praise his name; let all your thoughts, words, and works tend to his glory.
Set your heart firmly on him, and on other things only as they are in and from him.
Let your soul be filled with so entire a love of him that you may love nothing but for his sake.”
“Have a pure intention of heart, a steadfast regard to his glory in all your actions.”
“Fix your eye upon the blessed hope of your calling, and make all the things of the world serve it.”

For then, and not until then, is that “mind in us which was also in Christ Jesus,” when, in every motion of our heart, in every word of our tongue, in every work of our hands, we “pursue nothing but in relation to him, and in subordination to his pleasure”; when we, too, neither think, nor speak, nor act to fulfill our “own will, but the will of him who sent us”; when, whether we “eat, or drink, or whatever we do, we do all to the glory of God.”
“Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profits me nothing.”
1 Corinthians 13:3.
There is great reason to fear that it will one day be said of most of you who are present here, that this scripture, like all those you have heard before, profited you nothing.

Some, perhaps, are not serious enough to pay attention to it; some who do pay attention will not believe it; some who do believe it will still think it a hard saying, and so forget it as soon as they can; and of those few who receive it gladly for a time, some, having no root of humility or self-denial, will fall away when persecution arises because of the word, rather than suffer for it.

Indeed, even of those who pay attention to it, who believe, remember, yes, and receive it so deeply into their hearts that it takes root there, endures the heat of temptation, and begins to bear fruit, still not all will bring forth fruit to perfection.
The cares or pleasures of the world, and the desire for other things (perhaps not felt until then), will grow up with the word and choke it.
Nor am I who speak the word of God any more secure from these dangers than you who hear it.
I, too, have to lament “an evil heart of unbelief.”
And whenever God allows persecution to arise, yes, even if it were only the slight persecution of reproach, I may be the first to be offended.

Or, if I am enabled to endure this, yet if He should let loose the cares of the world upon me, or if He should cease to guard me against those pleasures that do not lead to Him, and the desire for other things [than knowing and loving Him], I would surely be overwhelmed, and, having preached to others, I myself would be a castaway.
Why then do I speak this word at all?
Why? Because a stewardship of the gospel has been committed to me: and though I do not know what I shall do tomorrow, today I will preach the gospel.

And with regard to you, my commission reads like this: “Son of man, I am sending you to them, and you shall say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord God’ — whether they will hear, or whether they will refrain.”
Thus says the Lord God: “Whoever you are who would enter into life, keep the commandments.”
(In order to do this, “believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved.”)
“Do not forsake the assembling together, as is the manner of some.”
In secret, likewise, “pray to your Father who sees in secret,” and “pour out your heart before Him.”
Make My word “a lantern to your feet and a light to your paths.”
Keep it “in your heart and in your mouth, when you sit in your house, when you walk by the way, when you lie down, and when you rise up.”
“Turn to Me with fasting,” as well as prayer; and, in obedience to your dying Redeemer, by eating that bread and drinking that cup, “show forth the Lord’s death until He comes.”

By the power you will receive from on high through these means, do all the things that are commanded in the Law, and avoid all those things that are forbidden in it, knowing that “if you offend in one point, you are guilty of all.”
“Do not forget to do good and to distribute” — yes, while you have time, do all the good you can to all men.
Then “deny yourself, take up your cross daily”; and, if called to it, “resist to the point of blood.”

And when each of you can say, “All this I have done,” then let him say further to himself (words at which not only someone like Felix, but the holiest soul on earth might tremble): “Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profits me nothing.”
It therefore concerns us all in the highest degree to know,
I. The full sense of those words, “Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned”;
II. The true meaning of the word love; and,
III. In what sense it can be said that without love all this profits us nothing.

I. As to the first: It must be observed that the word used by St. Paul properly means to divide into small pieces, and then to distribute what has been divided in this way; and consequently it implies not merely stripping ourselves all at once of all the worldly goods we enjoy, whether from a fit of distaste for the world or a sudden burst of devotion, but an act of choice, and that choice coolly and steadily carried out.
It may also imply that this is done not out of vanity, but in part from a right principle; namely, from a purpose to carry out the command of God, and a desire to obtain His kingdom.

It must further be observed that the word give means actually to deliver a thing according to agreement; and accordingly it implies, like the preceding word, not a hasty, thoughtless action, but one performed with open eyes and a determined heart, in keeping with a resolution taken beforehand.

The full sense of the words, therefore, is this — he who has ears to hear, let him hear: “Though I should give all the substance of my house to feed the poor; though I should do so after mature choice and deliberation; though I should spend my life in dealing it out to them with my own hands, yes, and that from a principle of obedience; though I should suffer, with the same aim, not only reproach and shame, not only bonds and imprisonment, and all this by my own continued act and deed, not accepting deliverance, but, moreover, death itself — yes, death inflicted in the manner most terrible to nature; yet with all this, if I do not have love (the love of God, and the love of all mankind, ‘shed abroad in my heart by the Holy Spirit given to me’), it profits me nothing.”
II. Let us inquire what this love is — what is the true meaning of the word?

We may consider it either with regard to its properties or its effects: and so that there may be no possibility of our being mistaken, we will not regard the judgment of men at all, but go to our Lord Himself for an account of the nature of love, and, for its effects, to His inspired Apostle.
The love which our Lord requires in all His followers is the love of God and man — of God for His own sake, and of man for God’s sake.

Now, what is it to love God, but to delight in Him, to rejoice in His will, to desire continually to please Him, to seek and find our happiness in Him, and to thirst day and night for a fuller enjoyment of Him?
As to the measure of this love, our Lord has clearly told us, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.”

Not that we are to love or delight in no one but Him: for He has commanded us not only to love our neighbor, that is, all men, as ourselves — to desire and pursue their happiness as sincerely and steadily as our own — but also to love many of His creatures in the strictest sense; to delight in them, to enjoy them: only in such a manner and measure as we know and feel not to unfit us for, but to prepare us for, the enjoyment of Him.
Thus, then, we are called to love God with all our heart.
The effects or properties of this love the Apostle describes in the chapter before us.
And since all these are infallible marks by which anyone may judge himself, whether he has this love or does not have it, they deserve our deepest consideration.
“Love suffers long,” or is longsuffering.

If you love your neighbor for God’s sake, you will bear long with his weaknesses: if he lacks wisdom, you will pity and not despise him; if he is in error, you will gently try to recover him, without any sharpness or reproach; if he is overtaken in a fault, you will labor to restore him in a spirit of meekness; and if perhaps that cannot be done soon, you will have patience with him, in case God may perhaps at length bring him to the knowledge and love of the truth.

In all provocations, whether from the weakness or the malice of men, you will show yourself a pattern of gentleness and meekness; and however often they are repeated, you will not be overcome by evil, but will overcome evil with good.
Let no one deceive you with empty words: he who is not longsuffering in this way does not have love.
Again: “Love is kind.”
Whoever feels the love of God and man shed abroad in his heart feels an ardent and uninterrupted thirst for the happiness of all his fellow creatures.
His soul melts away with the very fervent desire he continually has to promote it; and out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
On his tongue is the law of kindness.
The same is stamped on all his actions.
The flame within is continually working its way out, and spreading abroad more and more, in every act of goodwill to all with whom he has to do.
So that whether he thinks or speaks, or whatever he does, it all points to the same end — advancing, by every possible means, the happiness of all his fellow creatures.
Therefore do not deceive your own souls: he who is not kind in this way does not have love.
Further: “Love does not envy.”
This, indeed, is implied when it is said, “Love is kind.”
For kindness and envy are incompatible: they can no more live together than light and darkness.
If we earnestly desire all happiness for all, we cannot be grieved at the happiness of anyone.
The fulfilling of our desire will be sweet to our soul; so far will we be from being pained by it.
If we are always doing what good we can for our neighbor, and wishing we could do more, it is impossible that we should resent any good he receives: indeed, it will be the very joy of our heart.
However much, then, we may flatter ourselves or one another, he who envies does not have love.
It follows: “Love does not vaunt itself”; or rather, is not rash or hasty in judging: for this is indeed the true meaning of the word.
All who love their neighbor for God’s sake will not easily form a bad opinion of anyone to whom they wish all good, spiritual as well as temporal.

They cannot condemn him even in their heart without evidence; nor on slight evidence either; nor, indeed, on any evidence, without first, if possible, bringing him and his accuser face to face, or at least informing him of the accusation and letting him speak for himself.
Every one of you feels that he cannot help acting this way toward someone he tenderly loves.
Why, then, he who does not act this way does not have love.
I will mention only one more of the properties of this love: “Love is not puffed up.”
You cannot wrong someone you love: therefore, if you love God with all your heart, you cannot wrong Him so far as to rob Him of His glory, by taking to yourself what is due to Him alone.

You will acknowledge that all you are, and all you have, is His; that without Him you can do nothing; that He is your light and your life, your strength and your all; and that you are nothing, yes, less than nothing, before Him.
And if you love your neighbor as yourself, you will not be able to prefer yourself before him.
Indeed, you will no more be able to despise anyone than to hate him.
[Indeed, you will think every man better than yourself.]
As wax melts away before the fire, so pride melts away before love.
All haughtiness, whether of heart, speech, or behavior, vanishes where love prevails.
It brings down the proud looks of him who boasted in his strength, and makes him like a little child: distrustful of himself, willing to hear, glad to learn, easily convinced, easily persuaded.
And whoever is otherwise minded, let him give up all vain hope: he is puffed up, and so does not have love.
III. It remains to inquire in what sense it can be said that “though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, yes, though I give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profits me nothing.”

The chief sense of the words is doubtless this: that whatever we do, and whatever we suffer, if we are not renewed in the spirit of our mind by “the love of God shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit given to us,” we cannot enter into eternal life.
No one can enter there except by virtue of the covenant which God has given to man in the Son of His love.
But because general truths are less apt to affect us, let us consider one or two particulars with regard to which all we can do or suffer, if we do not have love, profits us nothing.
And, first, all this without love does not profit so as to make life happy; nor, second, so as to make death comfortable.
And first, without love nothing can profit us so as to make our lives happy.
By happiness I do not mean a slight, trifling pleasure that perhaps begins and ends in the same hour, but such a state of well-being as contents the soul and gives it a steady, lasting satisfaction.

But that nothing without love can profit us with respect to our present happiness will appear from this single consideration: you cannot lack it in any single instance without pain; and the further you depart from it, the greater the pain.
Are you lacking in longsuffering?
Then, so far as you fall short of this, you fall short of happiness.
The more the opposite dispositions — anger, irritability, revenge — prevail, the more unhappy you are.
You know it; you feel it; nor can the storm be calmed, or peace ever return to your soul, unless meekness, gentleness, patience — or, in one word, love — takes possession of it.
Does anyone find in himself ill will, malice, envy, or any other disposition opposed to kindness?
Then misery is there; and the stronger the disposition, the more miserable he is.
If the lazy man may be said to eat his own flesh, much more the malicious or envious man.
His soul is the very image of hell — full of torment as well as wickedness.
He already has the worm that never dies, and he is hastening to the fire that can never be quenched.
Only, as yet the great gulf is not fixed between him and heaven.

As yet there is a Spirit ready to help his weaknesses, who is still willing, if he stretches out his hands to heaven and laments his ignorance and misery, to purify his heart from vile affections, and to renew it in the love of God, and so lead him through present happiness up to eternal happiness.
Second: Without love, nothing can make death comfortable.
By comfortable I do not mean stupefied or senseless.
I would not say that he died comfortably who died of a stroke, or by a cannon shot, any more than he who, having his conscience seared, died as unconcerned as the beasts that perish.
Nor do I believe you would envy anyone the comfort of dying raving mad.
But by a comfortable death I mean a calm passage out of life, full of even, rational peace and joy.
And such a death all the doing and all the suffering in the world cannot give, without love.
To make this still more evident, I cannot appeal to your own experience; but I may appeal to what we have seen, and to the experience of others.
And I myself have seen two go out of this life in what I call a comfortable manner, though not with equal comfort.
One evidently had more comfort than the other, because he had more love.
I attended the first during a great part of his last trial, as well as when he yielded up his soul to God.
He cried out, “God chastens me with severe pain; but I thank Him for all; I bless Him for all; I love Him for all!”
When he was asked, not long before his release, “Are the consolations of God small to you?” he replied aloud, “No, no, no!”
Calling all who were near him by their names, he said, “Think of heaven, talk of heaven: all the time is lost when we are not thinking of heaven.”
Now this was the voice of love; and so far as that prevailed, all was comfort, peace, and joy.
But as his love was not perfect, neither was his comfort.
He had intervals of [anger or] irritability, and in them of misery; by both giving an indisputable proof that love can sweeten both life and death.
So when love is either absent from, or obscured in, the soul, there is no peace or comfort there.
It was in this place that I saw the other good soldier of Jesus Christ grappling with his last enemy, death.
And it was indeed a spectacle worthy to be seen by God, and angels, and men.
Some of his last breath was spent in a psalm of praise to Him who was then giving him the victory; in assurance of which he began to triumph even in the heat of the battle.
When he was asked, “Do you have the love of God in your heart?” he lifted up his eyes and hands, and answered, “Yes, yes!” with all the strength he had left.
To someone who asked if he was afraid of the devil, whom he had just mentioned as making his last attack on him, he replied, “No, no: my loving Savior has conquered every enemy: He is with me.
I fear nothing.” Soon after, he said, “The way to our loving Savior is sharp, but it is short.”
Nor was it long before he fell into a kind of slumber, in which his soul sweetly returned to God who gave it.
Here, we may observe, was no mixture of any passion or disposition contrary to love; therefore there was no misery, perfect love casting out whatever might have caused torment.
And whoever you are who have a like measure of love, your last end will be like his.

blocks.x: To the Reader:

s: Nothing but the strongest conviction, not only that what is set forth here is “the truth as it is in Jesus,” but also that I am absolutely bound to declare this truth to all the world, could have persuaded me openly to oppose the views of those whom I esteem for their work’s sake: at whose feet may I be found in the day of the Lord Jesus!
Should anyone believe it his duty to reply to this, I have only one request to make: let whatever you do be done from the heart, in love, and in the spirit of meekness.

Let your very disputing show that you have “put on, as the elect of God, a heart of mercy, gentleness, patience,” so that even at this time it may be said, “See how these Christians love one another!”
Whereas a pamphlet entitled “Free Grace Indeed” has been published against this sermon, this is to inform the publisher that I cannot answer his tract until he appears to be more in earnest.
For I dare not speak of “the deep things of God” in the spirit of a prize-fighter or a stage-player.
“He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how shall he not also with him freely give us all things?” Romans 8:32
1. How freely God loves the world!
While we were still sinners, “Christ died for the ungodly.”
While we were “dead in our sin,” God “did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.”
And how freely with him does he “give us all things”!
Truly, FREE GRACE is all in all!
2. The grace or love of God, from which our salvation comes, is FREE IN ALL, and FREE FOR ALL.
3. First. It is free in all to whom it is given.
It does not depend on any power or merit in man; no, not in any degree, neither in whole nor in part.
It does not in any way depend either on the good works or the righteousness of the receiver; not on anything he has done, or anything he is.
It does not depend on his efforts.
It does not depend on his good dispositions, or good desires, or good purposes and intentions; for all these flow from the free grace of God; they are only the streams, not the fountain.
They are the fruits of free grace, and not the root.
They are not the cause, but the effects of it.
Whatever good is in man, or is done by man, God is the author and doer of it.
Thus his grace is free in all; that is, in no way depending on any power or merit in man, but on God alone, who freely gave us his own Son, and “with him freely gives us all things.”
4. But it is free for ALL, as well as IN ALL.
To this some have answered, “No: it is free only for those whom God has ordained to life; and they are but a little flock.
The greater part of mankind God has ordained to death; and it is not free for them.
Them God hates; and therefore, before they were born, he decreed that they should die eternally.
And this he decreed absolutely; because such was his good pleasure; because it was his sovereign will.
Accordingly, they are born for this: to be destroyed body and soul in hell.
And they grow up under the irrevocable curse of God, without any possibility of redemption; for what grace God gives, he gives only for this: to increase, not prevent, their damnation.”
5. This is that decree of predestination.
But I think I hear someone say, “This is not the predestination which I hold: I hold only the election of grace.
What I believe is no more than this: that God, before the foundation of the world, elected a certain number of men to be justified, sanctified, and glorified.

Now, all these will be saved, and no one else; for the rest of mankind God leaves to themselves: so they follow the imaginations of their own hearts, which are only evil continually, and, growing worse and worse, are at length justly punished with everlasting destruction.”
6. Is this all the predestination which you hold?
Consider; perhaps this is not all.
Do you not believe that God ordained them to this very thing? If so, you believe the whole decree; you hold predestination in the full sense which has been described above.
But it may be you think you do not.
Do you not, then, believe that God hardens the hearts of those who perish? Do you not believe that he (literally) hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and that for this end he raised him up, or created him?
Why, this amounts to exactly the same thing.
If you believe that Pharaoh, or any one man on earth, was created for this end—to be damned—you hold all that has been said of predestination.

And there is no need for you to add that God backs up his decree, which is supposed to be unchangeable and irresistible, by hardening the hearts of those vessels of wrath whom that decree had previously fitted for destruction.

7. Well, but it may be you do not believe even this; you do not hold any decree of reprobation; you do not think God decrees any man to be damned, nor hardens him, nor irresistibly fits him for damnation; you only say, “God eternally decreed that, all being dead in sin, he would say to some of the dry bones, Live, and to others he would not; that, consequently, these should be made alive, and those remain in death—these should glorify God by their salvation, and those by their destruction.”
8. Is this not what you mean by the election of grace?
If it is, I would ask one or two questions: Are any who are not thus elected saved? Or have any been, from the foundation of the world?
Is it possible for any man to be saved unless he is thus elected?

If you say, “No,” you are just where you were; you have not moved one hair’s breadth farther; you still believe that, as a consequence of an unchangeable, irresistible decree of God, the greater part of mankind remain in death, without any possibility of redemption, inasmuch as no one can save them but God, and he will not save them.
You believe he has absolutely decreed not to save them; and what is this but decreeing to damn them?

It is, in effect, neither more nor less; it comes to the same thing; for if you are dead, and altogether unable to make yourself alive, then, if God has absolutely decreed that he will make only others alive, and not you, he has absolutely decreed your everlasting death; you are absolutely consigned to damnation.

So then, though you use softer words than some, you mean the very same thing; and God’s decree concerning the election of grace, according to your account of it, amounts to neither more nor less than what others call God’s decree of reprobation.
9. Call it therefore by whatever name you please—election, preterition, predestination, or reprobation—it comes in the end to the same thing.

The sense of them all is plainly this: by virtue of an eternal, unchangeable, irresistible decree of God, one part of mankind are infallibly saved, and the rest infallibly damned; it being impossible that any of the former should be damned, or that any of the latter should be saved.
10. But if this is so, then all preaching is in vain.
It is needless to those who are elected; for they, whether with preaching or without it, will infallibly be saved.

Therefore the purpose of preaching—to save souls—is void with regard to them; and it is useless to those who are not elected, for they cannot possibly be saved: they, whether with preaching or without it, will infallibly be damned.
The purpose of preaching is therefore void with regard to them likewise; so that in either case our preaching is in vain, as your hearing is also in vain.
11. This, then, is a plain proof that the doctrine of predestination is not a doctrine of God, because it makes void the ordinance of God; and God is not divided against himself.
A second is that it directly tends to destroy that holiness which is the aim of all the ordinances of God.

I do not say that none who hold it are holy (for God is of tender mercy to those who are unavoidably entangled in errors of any kind); but that the doctrine itself—that every man is either elected or not elected from eternity, and that the one must inevitably be saved, and the other inevitably damned—has a manifest tendency to destroy holiness in general; for it wholly takes away those first motives to pursue it which are so frequently set forth in Scripture: the hope of future reward and the fear of punishment, the hope of heaven and the fear of hell.

That these shall go away into everlasting punishment, and those into life eternal, is no motive to struggle for life to him who believes his lot is already cast; it is not reasonable for him to do so, if he thinks he is unalterably sentenced either to life or to death.
You will say, “But he does not know whether it is life or death.”

What then? This does not help the matter; for if a sick man knows that he must unavoidably die, or unavoidably recover, though he does not know which, it is unreasonable for him to take any medicine at all.

He might justly say (and so I have heard some speak, both in bodily sickness and in spiritual), “If I am ordained to life, I shall live; if to death, I shall die; so I need not trouble myself about it.”
So directly does this doctrine tend to shut the very gate of holiness in general—to hinder unholy men from ever approaching it, or striving to enter in by it.
12. Just as directly does this doctrine tend to destroy several particular branches of holiness.
Such are meekness and love—love, I mean, of our enemies—of the evil and unthankful.

I do not say that none who hold it have meekness and love (for as is the power of God, so is his mercy); but that it naturally tends to inspire, or increase, a sharpness or eagerness of temper which is quite contrary to the meekness of Christ, as then especially appears when they are opposed on this point.
And it just as naturally inspires contempt or coldness towards those whom we suppose to be outcasts from God.
“Oh, but,” you say,
“I suppose no particular man to be a reprobate.”
You mean you would not if you could help it: but you cannot help sometimes applying your general doctrine to particular persons; the enemy of souls will apply it for you.
You know how often he has done so.
But you rejected the thought with abhorrence.

True; as soon as you could; but how it soured and sharpened your spirit in the meantime! You know well that it was not the spirit of love which you then felt towards that poor sinner, whom you supposed or suspected, whether you would or not, to have been hated by God from eternity.
13. Thirdly. This doctrine tends to destroy the comfort of religion, the happiness of Christianity.
This is evident as to all those who believe themselves to be reprobated, or who only suspect or fear it.
All the great and precious promises are lost to them; they give them no ray of comfort: for they are not the elect of God; therefore they have neither lot nor portion in them.
This is an effective bar to their finding any comfort or happiness, even in that religion whose ways are designed to be “ways of pleasantness, and all her paths peace.”
14. And as to you who believe yourselves to be the elect of God, what is your happiness?

I hope, not a notion, a speculative belief, a bare opinion of any kind; but a felt possession of God in your heart, worked in you by the Holy Spirit, or the witness of God’s Spirit with your spirit that you are a child of God.
This, otherwise called “the full assurance of faith,” is the true ground of a Christian’s happiness.
And it does indeed imply a full assurance that all your past sins are forgiven, and that you are now a child of God.
But it does not necessarily imply a full assurance of our future perseverance.
I do not say this is never joined to it, but that it is not necessarily implied in it; for many have the one who do not have the other.

15. Now, experience shows this witness of the Spirit to be much obstructed by this doctrine; and not only in those who, believing themselves reprobated, thrust it far from them by this belief, but even in those who have tasted of that good gift, who yet have soon lost it again, and fallen back into doubts, and fears, and darkness—horrible darkness, that might be felt!
And I appeal to any of you who hold this doctrine to say, between God and your own hearts, whether you do not often have a return of doubts and fears concerning your election or perseverance!
If you ask, “Who does not?”

I answer, Very few of those who hold this doctrine; but many, very many, of those who do not hold it, in all parts of the earth—many of these have enjoyed the uninterrupted witness of his Spirit, the continual light of his countenance, from the moment in which they first believed, for many months or years, to this day.

16. That assurance of faith which these enjoy excludes all doubt and fear. It excludes all kinds of doubt and fear concerning their future perseverance, though it is not properly, as was said before, an assurance of what is future, but only of what now is.

And this does not need for its support a speculative belief that whoever is once ordained to life must live; for it is worked from hour to hour by the mighty power of God, “by the Holy Spirit who is given to them.”

And therefore that doctrine is not of God, because it tends to obstruct, if not destroy, this great work of the Holy Spirit, from which flows the chief comfort of religion, the happiness of Christianity.
17. Again: how uncomfortable a thought is this, that thousands and millions of men, without any preceding offence or fault of theirs, were unchangeably doomed to everlasting burnings!

How especially uncomfortable must it be to those who have put on Christ! To those who, being filled with a heart of mercy, tenderness, and compassion, could even “wish themselves accursed for their brethren’s sake”!
18. Fourthly. This uncomfortable doctrine directly tends to destroy our zeal for good works.
And this it does, first, as it naturally tends (according to what was observed before) to destroy our love for the greater part of mankind, namely, the evil and unthankful.
For whatever lessens our love must go far to lessen our desire to do them good.

This it does, secondly, as it cuts off one of the strongest motives to all acts of bodily mercy, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and the like—namely, the hope of saving their souls from death.
For what does it profit to relieve the earthly needs of those who are just dropping into eternal fire?
“Well; but run and snatch them as brands out of the fire.” No, this you suppose impossible.
They were appointed to it, you say, from eternity, before they had done either good or evil. You believe it is the will of God that they should die.
And “who has resisted his will?”
But you say you do not know whether these are elected or not.
What then? If you know they are the one or the other—that they are either elected or not elected—all your labour is void and vain.
In either case, your advice, reproof, or exhortation is as needless and useless as our preaching.
It is needless to those who are elected; for they will infallibly be saved without it.
It is useless to those who are not elected; for with or without it they will infallibly be damned; therefore you cannot, consistently with your principles, take any pains about their salvation.
Consequently, those principles directly tend to destroy your zeal for good works; for all good works, but particularly for the greatest of all, the saving of souls from death.
19. But, fifthly, this doctrine not only tends to destroy Christian holiness, happiness, and good works, but has also a direct and manifest tendency to overthrow the whole Christian Revelation.
The point which the wisest of the modern unbelievers most diligently labour to prove is that the Christian Revelation is not necessary.
They know well that, if they could once show this, the conclusion would be too plain to be denied: “If it is not necessary, it is not true.” Now, this fundamental point you give up.

For, supposing that eternal, unchangeable decree, one part of mankind must be saved though the Christian Revelation were not in existence, and the other part of mankind must be damned notwithstanding that Revelation.
And what more would an unbeliever desire?
You allow him all he asks.
In thus making the gospel unnecessary to all sorts of men, you give up the whole Christian cause.
“Oh, tell it not in Gath! lest the daughters of the uncircumcised rejoice”; lest the sons of unbelief triumph!
20. And as this doctrine manifestly and directly tends to overthrow the whole Christian Revelation, so it does the same thing, by plain consequence, in making that Revelation contradict itself.
For it is grounded on such an interpretation of some texts (more or fewer, it does not matter) as flatly contradicts all the other texts, and indeed the whole scope and tenor of Scripture.

For instance: the defenders of this doctrine interpret that text of Scripture, “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated,” as implying that God in a literal sense hated Esau, and all the reprobated, from eternity.
Now, what can possibly be a more flat contradiction than this, not only to the whole scope and tenor of Scripture, but also to all those particular texts which expressly declare, “God is love”?

Again: they infer from that text, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Romans 4:15), that God is love only to some men, namely, the elect, and that he has mercy for those only; flatly contrary to which is the whole tenor of Scripture, as is that express declaration in particular, “The Lord is loving to every man, and his mercy is over all his works.”

(Psalm 145:9) Again: they infer from that and similar texts, “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” that he shows mercy only to those whom he had regarded with favour from all eternity.
No, but who is replying against God now?
You now contradict the whole oracles of God, which declare throughout, “God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34); “There is no favouritism with him.”

(Romans 2:11) Again: from that text, “The children being not yet born, and having done neither good nor evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not by works, but by him who calls, it was said to her,” to Rebecca, “The elder shall serve the younger,” you infer that our being predestinated, or elect, in no way depends on the foreknowledge of God.
Flatly contrary to this are all the Scriptures, and those in particular: “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God” (1 Peter 1:2); “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestinated” (Romans 8:29).
21. And “the same Lord over all is rich” in mercy “to all who call upon him” (Romans 10:12). But you say, “No; he is such only to those for whom Christ died.
And those are not all, but only a few, whom God has chosen out of the world; for he did not die for all, but only for those who were ‘chosen in him before the foundation of the world.’”

(Ephesians 1:4) Flatly contrary to your interpretation of these scriptures, also, is the whole tenor of the New Testament, as are in particular those texts: “Do not destroy by your food him for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15)—a clear proof that Christ died not only for those who are saved, but also for those who perish. He is “the Saviour of the world” (John 4:42); he is “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29); “He is the propitiation, not for our sins only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2); “He,” the living God, “is the Saviour of all men” (1 Timothy 4:10); “He gave himself a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6); “He tasted death for every man” (Hebrews 2:9).

22. If you ask, “Why then are not all men saved?” the whole law and the testimony answer, first, not because of any decree of God; not because it is his pleasure that they should die; for, “As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies.”

(Ezekiel 18:3, 32) Whatever the cause of their perishing may be, it cannot be his will, if the oracles of God are true; for they declare, “He is not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9); “He wills that all men should be saved.”
And they, secondly, declare what the cause is why all men are not saved, namely, that they will not be saved: so our Lord expressly says, “You will not come to me that you might have life.”
(John 5:40) “The power of the Lord is present to heal” them, but they will not be healed.
“They reject the counsel,” the merciful counsel, “of God against themselves,” as did their stiff-necked forefathers.

And therefore they are without excuse; because God would save them, but they will not be saved: this is the condemnation, “How often would I have gathered you together, and you would not!” (Matthew 23:37).

23. Thus manifestly does this doctrine tend to overthrow the whole Christian Revelation, by making it contradict itself; by giving such an interpretation of some texts as flatly contradicts all the other texts, and indeed the whole scope and tenor of Scripture—an abundant proof that it is not of God.

But neither is this all: for, seventhly, it is a doctrine full of blasphemy; of such blasphemy as I should dread to mention, except that the honour of our gracious God, and the cause of his truth, will not allow me to be silent.
In the cause of God, then, and from a sincere concern for the glory of his great name, I will mention a few of the horrible blasphemies contained in this horrible doctrine.
But first, I must warn every one of you who hears, as you will answer for it at the great day, not to charge me (as some have done) with blaspheming because I mention the blasphemy of others.

And the more you are grieved with those who blaspheme in this way, see that you “confirm your love towards them” the more, and that your heart’s desire and continual prayer to God be, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do!”

24. This being stated first, let it be observed that this doctrine represents our blessed Lord, “Jesus Christ the righteous,” “the only begotten Son of the Father, full of grace and truth,” as a hypocrite, a deceiver of the people, a man void of common sincerity.
For it cannot be denied that he everywhere speaks as if he were willing that all men should be saved.
Therefore, to say he was not willing that all men should be saved is to represent him as a mere hypocrite and dissembler.
It cannot be denied that the gracious words which came out of his mouth are full of invitations to all sinners.
To say, then, that he did not intend to save all sinners is to represent him as a gross deceiver of the people.
You cannot deny that he says, “Come to me, all you who are weary and heavy laden.”
If, then, you say he calls those who cannot come; those whom he knows to be unable to come; those whom he can make able to come, but will not; how is it possible to describe greater insincerity?
You represent him as mocking his helpless creatures, by offering what he never intends to give.
You describe him as saying one thing and meaning another; as pretending a love which he did not have.

Him, in “whose mouth was no deceit,” you make full of deceit, void of common sincerity—then especially, when, drawing near the city, he wept over it and said, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets, and stone those who are sent to you; how often would I have gathered your children together—and you would not”; ēthelēsa kai ouk ēthelēsate.
Now, if you say they would, but he would not, you represent him (and who could bear to hear it?) as weeping crocodile tears; weeping over the prey which he himself had doomed to destruction!
25. Such blasphemy is this, as one would think might make the ears of a Christian tingle!
But there is yet more to come; for just as it honours the Son, so does this doctrine honour the Father.

It destroys all his attributes at once: it overturns his justice, mercy, and truth alike; yes, it represents the most holy God as worse than the devil, as both more false, more cruel, and more unjust.

More false, because the devil, liar as he is, has never said, “He wills all men to be saved.” More unjust, because the devil cannot, even if he would, be guilty of such injustice as you ascribe to God, when you say that God condemned millions of souls to everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels, for continuing in sin which, for want of that grace he will not give them, they cannot avoid. And more cruel, because that unhappy spirit “seeks rest and finds none,” so that his own restless misery is a kind of temptation to him to tempt others.

But God rests in his high and holy place; so that to suppose him, of his own mere impulse, of his pure will and pleasure, happy as he is, to doom his creatures, whether they will or not, to endless misery, is to impute to him such cruelty as we cannot impute even to the great enemy of God and man.
It is to represent the high God (he who has ears to hear, let him hear!) as more cruel, false, and unjust than the devil!
26. This is the blasphemy clearly contained in the horrible decree of predestination!
And here I plant my foot.
On this I take issue with every defender of it.
You represent God as worse than the devil; more false, more cruel, more unjust.
But you say you will prove it by Scripture.
Stop! What will you prove by Scripture? That God is worse than the devil?
It cannot be. Whatever that Scripture proves, it can never prove this, whatever its true meaning may be.
This cannot be its true meaning.
Do you ask, “What is its true meaning, then?”
If I say, “I do not know,” you have gained nothing; for there are many scriptures whose true sense neither you nor I shall know until death is swallowed up in victory.
But this I know: it would be better to say it had no sense at all than to say it had such a sense as this.
It cannot mean, whatever else it may mean, that the God of truth is a liar.
Let it mean what it will, it cannot mean that the Judge of all the world is unjust.
No scripture can mean that God is not love, or that his mercy is not over all his works; that is, whatever else it may prove, no scripture can prove predestination.

27. This is the blasphemy for which (however much I love the persons who assert it) I abhor the doctrine of predestination, a doctrine on the supposition of which, if one could possibly suppose it for a moment (call it election, reprobation, or what you please, for all comes to the same thing), one might say to our adversary the devil, “You fool, why do you roar about any longer?
Your lying in wait for souls is as needless and useless as our preaching.
Do you not hear that God has taken your work out of your hands, and that he does it much more effectively?
You, with all your principalities and powers, can only assault us in such a way that we may resist you; but He can irresistibly destroy both body and soul in hell!
You can only entice; but his unchangeable decree, to leave thousands of souls in death, compels them to continue in sin until they drop into everlasting burnings.
You tempt; He forces us to be damned; for we cannot resist his will.
You fool, why do you go about any longer, seeking whom you may devour?

Do you not hear that God is the devouring lion, the destroyer of souls, the murderer of men? Moloch caused only children to pass through the fire, and that fire was soon quenched; or, the corruptible body being consumed, its torment was at an end; but God, you are told, by his eternal decree, fixed before they had done good or evil, causes not only children a span long, but the parents also, to pass through the fire of hell, the ‘fire which shall never be quenched’; and the body which is cast into it, being now incorruptible and immortal, will be ever consuming and never consumed, but ‘the smoke of their torment,’ because it is God’s good pleasure, ‘ascends up for ever and ever.’”
28. Oh, how the enemy of God and man would rejoice to hear that these things were so!
How he would cry aloud and not hold back!
How he would lift up his voice and say, “To your tents, O Israel!
Flee from the face of this God, or you will utterly perish!
But where will you flee?
Into heaven? He is there. Down to hell?
He is there also.
You cannot flee from an omnipresent, almighty tyrant.
And whether you flee or stay, I call heaven, his throne, and earth, his footstool, to witness against you: you shall perish, you shall die eternally.
Sing, O hell, and rejoice, you who are under the earth!
For God, even the mighty God, has spoken, and devoted to death thousands of souls, from the rising of the sun to its going down!
Here, O death, is your sting!
They shall not, cannot escape; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it.
Here, O grave, is your victory! Nations yet unborn, before ever they have done good or evil, are doomed never to see the light of life, but you shall gnaw upon them for ever and ever!
Let all those morning stars sing together who fell with Lucifer, son of the morning!
Let all the sons of hell shout for joy!
For the decree is passed, and who shall annul it?”
29. Yes, the decree is passed; and so it was before the foundation of the world.
But what decree? Even this: “I will set before the sons of men ‘life and death, blessing and cursing.’
And the soul that chooses life shall live, as the soul that chooses death shall die.”

This decree, by which “those whom God foreknew, he predestinated,” was indeed from everlasting; this decree, by which all who allow Christ to make them alive are “elect according to the foreknowledge of God,” now stands fast, even as the moon, and as the faithful witnesses in heaven; and when heaven and earth pass away, yet this shall not pass away; for it is as unchangeable and eternal as is the being of God who gave it.
This decree yields the strongest encouragement to abound in all good works and in all holiness; and it is a wellspring of joy, and of happiness also, to our great and endless comfort.
This is worthy of God; it is in every way consistent with all the perfections of his nature.
It gives us the noblest view of his justice, mercy, and truth alike.
With this agrees the whole scope of the Christian Revelation, as well as all its parts.

To this Moses and all the Prophets bear witness, and our blessed Lord and all his Apostles. Thus Moses, in the name of his Lord: “I call heaven and earth to record against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live.”
Thus Ezekiel (to cite one prophet for all): “The soul that sins, it shall die: the son shall not bear” eternally “the iniquity of the father.
The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.”
(Ezekiel 18:20) Thus our blessed Lord: “If any man is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.”
(John 7:37) Thus his great Apostle, St. Paul (Acts 17:30): “God commands all men everywhere to repent”—“all men everywhere”: every man in every place, without any exception either of place or person.
Thus St. James: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all men liberally, and does not reproach, and it shall be given him.”
(James 1:5) Thus St. Peter (2 Peter 3:9): “The Lord is not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.”
And thus St. John: “If any man sins, we have an Advocate with the Father; and he is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world.”
30. Oh, hear this, you who forget God!
You cannot lay your death at his door! “‘Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die?’ says the Lord God.”
(Ezekiel 18:23ff.) “Repent, and turn from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin.
Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed—for why will you die, O house of Israel?
For I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies, says the Lord God.
Therefore turn yourselves, and live.”
“As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked.—Turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11)
“You almost persuade me to be a Christian.” Acts 26:28.
And there are many who go this far: ever since the Christian religion has been in the world, there have been many in every age and nation who were almost persuaded to be Christians.
But seeing that it avails nothing before God to go only this far, it greatly concerns us to consider,
First, what is implied in being almost,
Secondly, what is implied in being altogether, a Christian.
I. (I.) 1. Now, being almost a Christian implies, first, heathen honesty.

No one, I suppose, will question this; especially since by heathen honesty here I mean not only that which is recommended in the writings of their philosophers, but such as the common heathen expected of one another, and many of them actually practised.

By its rules they were taught that they ought not to be unjust; not to take away their neighbour’s goods, either by robbery or theft; not to oppress the poor, nor to use extortion toward anyone; not to cheat or overreach either the poor or the rich, in whatever dealings they had with them; to defraud no one of his right; and, if it were possible, to owe no one anything.
2. Again, the common heathen allowed that some regard was to be paid to truth, as well as to justice.

And accordingly they held in abomination not only him who perjured himself, who called God to witness to a lie, but also him who was known to be a slanderer of his neighbour, who falsely accused anyone.
And indeed, they thought little better of deliberate liars of any sort, regarding them as the disgrace of humankind and the pests of society.
3. Yet again, there was a kind of love and assistance which they expected from one another.
They expected whatever assistance anyone could give another without harm to himself.

And this they extended not only to those little offices of humanity which are performed without any expense or labour, but also to feeding the hungry, if they had food to spare; clothing the naked with their own surplus clothing; and, in general, giving to anyone in need such things as they did not need themselves.
This far, by the lowest account of it, heathen honesty went; the first thing implied in being almost a Christian.
(II.) 4. A second thing implied in being almost a Christian is having a form of godliness—of that godliness which is prescribed in the gospel of Christ; having the outside of a real Christian.

Accordingly, the almost Christian does nothing which the gospel forbids. He does not take the name of God in vain; he blesses and does not curse; he does not swear at all, but his speech is, Yes, yes; No, no. He does not profane the Lord’s Day, nor allow it to be profaned, even by the stranger who is within his gates. He not only avoids all actual adultery, fornication, and uncleanness, but every word or look that either directly or indirectly tends toward them; yes, and all idle words, abstaining from detraction, backbiting, talebearing, and evil speaking, and from “all foolish talking and jesting”—eutrapelia, a kind of virtue in the heathen moralist’s account—in short, from all conversation that is not “good for the purpose of edifying,” and that consequently “grieves the Holy Spirit of God, by whom we are sealed to the day of redemption.”
5. He abstains from “wine in which is excess”; from revelries and gluttony.
He avoids, as far as lies in him, all strife and contention, continually endeavouring to live peaceably with all men.

And if he suffers wrong, he does not avenge himself, nor return evil for evil. He is no reviler, no brawler, no scoffer, either at the faults or the weaknesses of his neighbour. He does not willingly wrong, hurt, or grieve anyone; but in all things acts and speaks by that plain rule, “Whatever you would not have him do to you, do not do to another.”
6. And in doing good, he does not confine himself to cheap and easy acts of kindness, but labours and suffers for the benefit of many, that by all means he may help some.
In spite of toil or pain, “whatever his hand finds to do, he does it with his might,” whether it is for his friends or for his enemies, for the evil or for the good.

For being “not slothful” in this, or in any “business,” as he “has opportunity” he does “good,” all kinds of good, “to all men,” and to their souls as well as their bodies. He reproves the wicked, instructs the ignorant, confirms the wavering, enlivens the good, and comforts the afflicted. He labours to awaken those who sleep; to lead those whom God has already awakened to the “Fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness,” that they may wash in it and be clean; and to stir up those who are saved through faith to adorn the gospel of Christ in all things.

7. He who has the form of godliness also uses the means of grace; yes, all of them, and at every opportunity. He constantly attends the house of God; and that not as some are in the habit of doing, who come into the presence of the Most High either loaded with gold and costly clothing, or in all the gaudy vanity of dress, and who, either by their untimely civilities to one another or the unfitting levity of their behaviour, disclaim all pretensions to the form as well as to the power of godliness.

Would to God there were none even among ourselves who fall under the same condemnation! who come into this house, perhaps, gazing about, or with all the signs of the most listless, careless indifference, though sometimes they may seem to use a prayer to God for his blessing on what they are entering upon; who, during that awe-inspiring service, are either asleep, or reclining in the most convenient posture for it; or, as though they supposed God was asleep, are talking with one another, or looking around, as if utterly without anything to do.
Nor let these be accused of having the form of godliness.
No; he who has even this behaves with seriousness and attention in every part of that solemn service.

More especially, when he approaches the table of the Lord, it is not with light or careless behaviour, but with an air, gesture, and bearing which speaks nothing else but “God be merciful to me a sinner!”
