s: Confirm, then, your love toward him, and you will thereby “heap coals of fire on his head.”
2. But see that the manner in which you speak is also according to the gospel of Christ.
Avoid everything in look, gesture, word, and tone of voice that smacks of pride or self-sufficiency.
Carefully avoid everything magisterial or dogmatic, everything that looks like arrogance or presumption.
Beware of the most distant approach to disdain, domineering, or contempt.
With equal care avoid all appearance of anger; and though you use great plainness of speech, yet let there be no reproach, no railing accusation, no sign of any warmth but that of love.

Above all, let there be no shadow of hate or ill will, no bitterness or sourness of expression; but use the air and language of sweetness as well as gentleness, so that all may appear to flow from love in the heart.

And yet this sweetness need not hinder you from speaking in the most serious and solemn manner; as far as possible, in the very words of the oracles of God (for there are none like them), and as under the eye of Him who is coming to judge the living and the dead.

3. If you do not have an opportunity of speaking to him in person, or cannot have access, you may do it by a messenger: by a mutual friend in whose prudence as well as uprightness you can thoroughly confide.
Such a person, speaking in your name, and in the spirit and manner described above, may answer the same end and, to a good degree, make up for your lack of service.
Only beware that you do not pretend a lack of opportunity in order to shun the cross; nor take it for granted that you cannot have access, without ever making the attempt.
Whenever you can speak in your own person, it is far better.
But you should rather do it through another than not at all: this way is better than none.
4. But what if you can neither speak yourself nor find such a messenger as you can confide in?
If this is really the case, it then only remains to write.
And there may be some circumstances which make this the most advisable way of speaking.
One of these circumstances is when the person with whom we have to deal is of so warm and impetuous a temper that he does not easily bear reproof, especially from an equal or an inferior.
But it may be so introduced and softened in writing as to make it far more tolerable.
Besides, many will read the very same words which they could not bear to hear.
It does not give so violent a shock to their pride, nor touch their honor so keenly.
And suppose it makes little impression at first, they will perhaps give it a second reading and, upon further consideration, lay to heart what they disregarded before.
If you add your name, this is nearly the same thing as going to him and speaking in person.
And this should always be done, unless it is made improper by some very particular reason.
5. It should be well observed, not only that this is a step which our Lord absolutely commands us to take, but that He commands us to take this step first, before we attempt any other.
No alternative is allowed, no choice of anything else: this is the way; walk in it.

It is true, He directs us, if need requires, to take two other steps; but they are to be taken successively after this step, and neither of them before it: much less are we to take any other step, either before this or besides it.
To do anything else, or not to do this, is therefore equally inexcusable.
6. Do not think to excuse yourself for taking an entirely different step by saying, “Why, I did not speak to anyone until I was so burdened that I could not refrain.”
You were burdened! It was no wonder that you should be, unless your conscience was seared; for you were under the guilt of sin, of disobeying a plain commandment of God!
You ought immediately to have gone and told “your brother of his fault between you and him alone.”
If you did not, how could you be anything but burdened (unless your heart was utterly hardened), while you were trampling the command of God underfoot, and “hating your brother in your heart”?
And what a way have you found to unburden yourself?

God reproves you for a sin of omission, for not telling your brother of his fault; and you comfort yourself under His reproof by a sin of commission, by telling your brother’s fault to another person!
Ease bought by sin is a costly purchase!
I trust in God that you will have no ease, but will be burdened all the more, until you “go to your brother and tell him,” and no one else.
7. I know of only one exception to this rule: there may be a peculiar case in which it is necessary to accuse the guilty, though absent, in order to preserve the innocent.
For instance: you are acquainted with the design which a man has against the property or life of his neighbor.
Now, the case may be so circumstanced that there is no other way of hindering that design from taking effect but by making it known, without delay, to him against whom it is laid.

In this case, therefore, this rule is set aside, as is that of the apostle, “Speak evil of no man”; and it is lawful, indeed, it is our bounden duty, to speak evil of an absent person, in order to prevent his doing evil to others and to himself at the same time.
But remember, meanwhile, that all evil-speaking is, in its own nature, deadly poison.

Therefore, if you are sometimes compelled to use it as a medicine, yet use it with fear and trembling, seeing it is so dangerous a medicine that nothing but absolute necessity can excuse your using it at all.
Accordingly, use it as seldom as possible, never except when there is such a necessity; and even then use as little of it as possible, only as much as is necessary for the intended end.
At all other times, “go and tell him of his fault between you and him alone.”
II. 1. But what “if he will not hear”?
If he repays evil for good?
If he is enraged rather than convinced?
What if he hears to no purpose, and still goes on in the evil of his way?
We must expect this will frequently be the case; the mildest and tenderest reproof will have no effect; but the blessing we wished for another will return into our own bosom.
And what are we to do then?
Our Lord has given us a clear and full direction.
Then “take with you one or two more”: this is the second step.
Take one or two whom you know to be of a loving spirit, lovers of God and of their neighbor.
See, likewise, that they are of a lowly spirit, and “clothed with humility.”
Let them also be such as are meek and gentle, patient and longsuffering; not apt to “return evil for evil, or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing.”
Let them be men of understanding, such as are endowed with wisdom from above; and unbiased men, free from partiality, free from prejudice of any kind.
Care should likewise be taken that both the persons and their characters are well known to him; and let those who are acceptable to him be chosen in preference to any others.
2. Love will dictate the manner in which they should proceed, according to the nature of the case.
Nor can any one particular manner be prescribed for all cases.

But perhaps, in general, one might advise that before they enter upon the matter itself, they mildly and affectionately declare that they have no anger or prejudice toward him, and that it is merely from a principle of goodwill that they now come, or concern themselves at all with his affairs.

To make this the more apparent, they might then calmly listen to your repetition of your former conversation with him, and to what he said in his own defense, before they attempted to determine anything.

After this they would be better able to judge in what manner to proceed, “that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might be established”; that whatever you have said may have its full force by the additional weight of their authority.
3. To this end, may they not (1)
Briefly repeat what you said, and what he answered?
(2) Enlarge upon, explain, and confirm the reasons which you had given?
(3) Give weight to your reproof, showing how just, how kind, and how timely it was?
And, lastly, enforce the advice and persuasions which you had attached to it?
And these may likewise hereafter, if need should require, bear witness to what was spoken.
4. With regard to this, as well as the preceding rule, we may observe that our Lord gives us no choice, leaves us no alternative, but expressly commands us to do this, and nothing else in its place.
He likewise directs us when to do this, neither sooner nor later: namely, after we have taken the first step, and before we have taken the third.
It is only then that we are authorized to relate the evil another has done to those whom we desire to take part with us in this great instance of brotherly love.
But let us take care how we relate it to any other person until both these steps have been taken.
If we neglect to take these, or if we take any others, what wonder if we are burdened still?
For we are sinners against God and against our neighbor; and however fairly we may color it, yet, if we have any conscience, our sin will find us out and bring a burden upon our soul.
III. 1. That we may be thoroughly instructed in this weighty affair, our Lord has given us a still further direction: “If he will not hear them,” then, and not until then, “tell it to the church.”
This is the third step.
The whole question is how this word, “the church,” is to be understood here.
But the very nature of the thing will determine this beyond all reasonable doubt.
You cannot tell it to the national Church, the whole body of people called “the Church of England.”
Nor would it answer any Christian end if you could; this, therefore, is not the meaning of the word.
Neither can you tell it to that whole body of people in England with whom you have a more immediate connection.
Nor, indeed, would this answer any good end: the word, therefore, is not to be understood this way.
It would not answer any valuable end to tell the faults of every particular member to the church (if you would call it that), the congregation or society united together in London.

It remains that you tell it to the elder or elders of the church, to those who are overseers of that flock of Christ to which you both belong, who watch over your soul and his, “as those who must give account.”
And this should be done, if it conveniently can, in the presence of the person concerned, and, though plainly, yet with all the tenderness and love which the nature of the thing will allow.
It properly belongs to their office to decide concerning the behavior of those under their care, and to rebuke, according to the demerit of the offense, “with all authority.”

When, therefore, you have done this, you have done all that the word of God, or the law of love, requires of you: you are not now a partaker of his sin; but if he perishes, his blood is on his own head.

2. Here, also, let it be observed that this, and no other, is the third step which we are to take; and that we are to take it in its order after the other two; not before the second, much less the first, unless in some very particular circumstance.
Indeed, in one case, the second step may coincide with this: they may be, in a manner, one and the same.

The elder or elders of the church may be so connected with the offending brother that they may set aside the necessity, and take the place, of the one or two witnesses; so that it may suffice to tell it to them after you have told it to your brother, “between you and him alone.”
3. When you have done this, you have delivered your own soul.
“If he will not hear the church,” if he persists in his sin, “let him be to you as a heathen man and a tax collector.”
You are under no obligation to think of him any more, except when you commend him to God in prayer.
You need not speak of him any more, but leave him to his own Master.
Indeed, you still owe him, as you owe all other heathens, earnest, tender goodwill.
You owe him courtesy and, as occasion offers, all the offices of humanity.
But have no friendship, no familiarity with him; no other dealings than with an open heathen.
4. But if this is the rule by which Christians walk, which is the land where Christians live?
You may possibly find a few scattered here and there who make it a matter of conscience to observe it.
But how very few!
How thinly scattered over the face of the earth!
And where is there any body of people that universally walks by it?
Can we find them in Europe?
Or, to go no further, in Great Britain or Ireland?
I fear not: I fear we may search these kingdoms throughout, and yet search in vain.
Alas for the Christian world!
Alas for Protestants, for Reformed Christians!
Oh, “who will rise up with me against the wicked?”
“Who will take God’s part” against the evil-speakers?
Are you the man?
By the grace of God, will you be one who is not carried away by the torrent?
Are you fully determined, God being your helper, from this very hour to set a watch, a continual “watch, before your mouth, and keep the door of your lips”?
From this hour will you walk by this rule, “Speaking evil of no man”?
If you see your brother do evil, will you “tell him of his fault between you and him alone”?
Afterwards, “take one or two witnesses,” and only then “tell it to the church”?
If this is the full purpose of your heart, then learn one lesson well: “Hear evil of no man.”
If there were no hearers, there would be no speakers, of evil.
And is not (according to the common proverb) the receiver as bad as the thief?
If, then, anyone begins to speak evil in your hearing, check him immediately.

Refuse to hear the voice of the charmer, however sweetly he charms; let him use ever so soft a manner, so mild an accent, ever so many professions of goodwill for the one whom he is stabbing in the dark, whom he strikes under the fifth rib!
Resolutely refuse to hear, though the whisperer complains of being “burdened till he speaks.”
Burdened! You fool! Are you in labor with your cursed secret, as a woman is in labor with child?
Go, then, and be delivered of your burden in the way the Lord has ordained!

First, “go and tell your brother of his fault between you and him alone”; next, “take with you one or two” mutual friends, and tell him in their presence; if neither of these steps takes effect, then “tell it to the church.”
But, at the peril of your soul, tell it to no one else, either before or after, except in that one exempted case, when it is absolutely necessary to preserve the innocent!
Why should you burden another as well as yourself, by making him a partaker of your sin?
5. Oh, that all of you who bear the reproach of Christ, who are in derision called Methodists, would set an example to the so-called Christian world, at least in this one instance!
Put away evil-speaking, tale-bearing, whispering: let none of them proceed out of your mouth!
See that you “speak evil of no man”; of the absent, nothing but good.
If you must be distinguished, whether you want to be or not, let this be the distinguishing mark of a Methodist: “He censures no man behind his back: by this fruit you may know him.”
What a blessed effect of this self-denial we would quickly feel in our hearts!
How would our “peace flow like a river,” when we thus “followed peace with all men”!
How would the love of God abound in our own souls, while we thus confirmed our love to our brethren!
And what an effect it would have on all who were united together in the name of the Lord Jesus!
How would brotherly love continually increase, when this great hindrance to it was removed!
All the members of Christ’s mystical body would then naturally care for each other.
“If one member suffered, all would suffer with it; if one was honored, all would rejoice with it”; and everyone would love his brother “with a pure heart fervently.”
Nor is this all: what an effect this might have even on the wild, unthinking world!

How soon would they discover in us what they could not find among all the thousands of their brethren, and cry (as Julian the Apostate did to his heathen courtiers), “See how these Christians love one another!”

By this chiefly would God convince the world, and prepare them also for His kingdom; as we may easily learn from those remarkable words in our Lord’s last, solemn prayer: “I pray for those who will believe in Me, that they all may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You; that the world may believe that You have sent Me!”
[John 17:21] May the Lord hasten the time!
May the Lord enable us thus to love one another, not only “in word and in tongue, but in deed and in truth,” even as Christ has loved us.
“Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his!” Numbers 23:10.
1. “Let my last end be like his!”
How many of you join in this wish?
Perhaps there are few of you who do not, even in this great congregation!
And oh, that this wish may rest upon your minds! — that it may not die away until your souls also are lodged “where the wicked cease from troubling, and where the weary are at rest!”
2. A detailed exposition of the text will not be expected on this occasion.
It would keep you too long from the sad yet pleasing thought of your beloved brother, friend, and pastor; yes, and father too: for how many are here whom he has “begotten in the Lord!”

Will it not, then, be more suited to your inclinations, as well as to this solemn occasion, to speak directly of this man of God, whom you have so often heard speaking in this place? — the end of whose conduct you know, “Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, and today, and forever.”
And may we not,
I. Observe a few particulars of his life and death?
II. Take some view of his character? and,
III. Inquire how we may make good use of this solemn providence, his sudden removal from us?
1. We may, in the first place, observe a few particulars of his life and death.
He was born at Gloucester in December 1714, and was put to a grammar school there when he was about twelve years old.
When he was seventeen, he began to be seriously religious, and served God to the best of his knowledge.

At about eighteen he went up to the University and was admitted to Pembroke College in Oxford; and about a year later he became acquainted with the Methodists (so called), whom from that time on he loved as his own soul.
2. Through them he was convinced that we “must be born again,” or outward religion will profit us nothing.

He joined with them in fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays; in visiting the sick and the prisoners; and in gathering up the very fragments of time, so that no moment might be lost: and he changed the course of his studies, reading chiefly such books as entered into the heart of religion and led directly to an experiential knowledge of Jesus Christ, and Him crucified.
3. He was soon tried as if by fire.
Not only was his reputation lost, and some of his dearest friends forsook him; but he was also tested by inward trials, and those of the severest kind.
Many nights he lay sleepless upon his bed; many days, prostrate on the ground.

But after he had groaned for several months under “the spirit of bondage,” God was pleased to remove the heavy load by giving him “the Spirit of adoption,” enabling him, through a living faith, to lay hold of “the Son of His love.”
4. However, it was thought necessary, for the recovery of his health, which was much impaired, that he should go into the country.
He accordingly went to Gloucester, where God enabled him to awaken several young people.
These soon formed themselves into a little society, and were some of the firstfruits of his labor.
Shortly afterward he began to read, two or three times a week, to some poor people in the town; and every day to read to and pray with the prisoners in the county jail.
5. Being now about twenty-one years of age, he was urged to enter into holy orders.
He was greatly afraid of this, being deeply aware of his own insufficiency.

But when the Bishop himself sent for him and told him, “Though I had intended to ordain no one under twenty-three, yet I will ordain you whenever you come” — and several other providential circumstances came together — he submitted, and was ordained on Trinity Sunday, 1736.
The next Sunday he preached to a crowded congregation in the church in which he had been baptized.
The following week he returned to Oxford and took his Bachelor’s degree: and he was now fully occupied, the care of the prisoners and the poor resting chiefly on him.
6. But it was not long before he was invited to London, to serve the parish of a friend who was going into the country.
He stayed there two months, lodging in the Tower, reading prayers in the chapel twice a week, catechizing and preaching once, besides visiting the soldiers in the barracks and the infirmary.
He also read prayers every evening at the Wapping chapel, and preached at Ludgate prison every Tuesday.

While he was here, letters came from his friends in Georgia which made him long to go and help them: but not seeing his call clearly, at the appointed time he returned to his little charge at Oxford, where several young men met daily in his room to build each other up in their most holy faith.
7. But he was soon called away from there again, to supply the parish of Dummer, in Hampshire.
Here he read prayers twice a day: early in the morning, and in the evening after the people came home from work.
He also catechized the children daily, and visited from house to house.
He now divided the day into three parts, allotting eight hours for sleep and meals, eight for study and solitude, and eight for reading prayers, catechizing, and visiting the people.
Is there a more excellent way for a servant of Christ and His Church?
If not, who will “go and do likewise”?

8. Yet his mind still ran on going abroad; and being now fully convinced that he was called by God to it, he set all things in order and, in January 1737, went down to take leave of his friends in Gloucester.
It was on this journey that God began to bless his ministry in an uncommon way.

Wherever he preached — in Gloucester, in Stonehouse, in Bath, in Bristol — amazing multitudes of hearers flocked together, so that the heat in the churches was scarcely bearable: and the impressions made on the minds of many were no less extraordinary.
After his return to London, while he was detained by General Oglethorpe from week to week and from month to month, it pleased God to bless his word still more.

And he was tireless in his labor: generally on Sunday he preached four times, to exceedingly large congregations, besides reading prayers two or three times, and often walking back and forth ten or twelve miles.
9. On December 28 he left London.
It was on the 29th that he first preached without notes.
On December 30 he went on board; but it was over a month before they were clear of the land.
One happy effect of their very slow passage he mentions the following April: “Blessed be God, we now live very comfortably in the great cabin.
We talk of little else but God and Christ; and scarcely a word is heard among us when we are together but what has reference to our fall in the first, and our new birth in the Second, Adam.”

It seems, likewise, to have been a special providence that he should spend a little time at Gibraltar, where both citizens and soldiers, high and low, young and old, acknowledged the day of their visitation.

10. From Sunday, May 7, 1738, until the latter end of the following August, he “made full proof of his ministry” in Georgia, particularly at Savannah: he read prayers and expounded twice a day, and visited the sick daily.
On Sunday he expounded at five in the morning; at ten he read prayers and preached, and again at three in the afternoon; and at seven in the evening he expounded the Church Catechism.
How much easier it is for our brethren in the ministry, whether in England, Scotland, or Ireland, to find fault with such a laborer in our Lord’s vineyard than to walk in his steps!

11. It was now that he observed the deplorable condition of many children here, and that God put into his heart the first thought of founding an Orphan House, for which he resolved to raise contributions in England, if God should give him a safe return there.
The following December he did return to London; and on Sunday, January 14, 1739, he was ordained priest at Christ Church, Oxford.
The next day he came to London again; and on Sunday the 21st he preached twice.
But though the churches were large and exceedingly crowded, yet many hundreds stood in the churchyard, and hundreds more went back home.
This first set him thinking of preaching in the open air.
But when he mentioned it to some of his friends, they judged it to be sheer madness: so he did not carry it out until after he had left London.

It was on Wednesday, February 21, that, finding all the church doors shut in Bristol (besides the fact that no church was able to hold half the congregation), at three in the afternoon he went to Kingswood and preached in the open air to nearly two thousand people.
On Friday he preached there to four or five thousand; and on Sunday to, it was supposed, ten thousand!
The number continually increased all the time he stayed at Bristol; and a flame of holy love was kindled which will not easily be put out.
The same was afterward kindled in various parts of Wales, of Gloucestershire, and of Worcestershire.
Indeed, wherever he went, God abundantly confirmed the word of His messenger.
12. On Sunday, April 29, he preached for the first time in Moorfields and on Kennington Common; and the thousands of hearers were as quiet as they could have been in a church.
Being again detained in England from month to month, he made little excursions into several counties, and received the contributions of willing multitudes for an Orphan House in Georgia.
The embargo that was now laid on shipping gave him leisure for more journeys through various parts of England, for which many will have reason to bless God to all eternity.
At length, on August 14, he embarked: but he did not land in Pennsylvania until October 30.

Afterward he went through Pennsylvania, the Jerseys, New York, Maryland, Virginia, and North and South Carolina, preaching all along the way to immense congregations, with fully as great an effect as in England.
On January 10, 1740, he arrived at Savannah.
13. On January 29 he added three desolate orphans to the nearly twenty whom he had in his house before.
The next day he laid out the ground for the house, about ten miles from Savannah.
On February 11 he took in four more orphans, and set out for Frederica in order to fetch the orphans who were in the southern parts of the colony.
On his return he established a school, both for children and for grown people, at Darien, and took four orphans from there.
On March 25 he laid the first stone of the Orphan House, to which, with great fitness, he gave the name Bethesda; a work for which children yet unborn shall praise the Lord.
He now had about forty orphans, so that there were nearly a hundred mouths to be fed daily.
But he was “anxious about nothing,” casting his care on Him who feeds the young ravens that call upon Him.
14. In April he made another tour through Pennsylvania, the Jerseys, and New York.
Incredible multitudes flocked to hear, among whom were a great many Black people.
In all places the greater part of the hearers were moved to an amazing degree.
Many were deeply convinced of their lost state; many were truly converted to God.

In some places thousands cried out aloud; many as if in the agonies of death; most were drowned in tears; some turned pale as death; others were wringing their hands; others lying on the ground; others sinking into the arms of their friends; almost all lifting up their eyes and calling for mercy.
15. He returned to Savannah on June 5.

The next evening, during the public service, the whole congregation, young and old, dissolved in tears: after the service several of the parishioners, and all his family, especially the little children, went home crying along the street, and some could not help praying aloud.
The groans and cries of the children continued all night, and for a great part of the next day.
16. In August he set out again, and came through various provinces to Boston.

While he was here and in the neighboring places, he was extremely weak in body: yet the multitudes of hearers were so great, and the effects produced in them so astonishing, that the oldest men then alive in the town had never seen the like before.
The same power attended his preaching at New York, particularly on Sunday, November 2: almost as soon as he began, crying, weeping, and wailing were to be heard on every side.
Many sank down to the ground, cut to the heart; and many were filled with divine consolation.

Toward the close of his journey he made this reflection: “It is the seventy-fifth day since I arrived at Rhode Island, exceedingly weak in body; yet God has enabled me to preach a hundred and seventy-five times in public, besides exhorting frequently in private!
Never did God grant me greater comforts: never did I make my journeys with less fatigue, or see such a continuance of the divine presence in the congregations to whom I preached.”
In December he returned to Savannah, and the following March he arrived in England.
17. You may easily observe that the preceding account is chiefly drawn from his own journals, which, for their artless and unaffected simplicity, may rival any writings of their kind.

And how exact a sample this is of his labors, both in Europe and America, for the honor of his beloved Master, during the thirty years that followed, as well as of the uninterrupted shower of blessings with which God was pleased to prosper his labors!
Is it not much to be lamented that anything should have prevented him from continuing this account, at least until near the time when he was called by his Lord to enjoy the fruit of his labor?
If he has left any papers of this kind, and his friends count me worthy of the honor, it would be my glory and joy to arrange, transcribe, and prepare them for publication.
18. A detailed account of the last scene of his life is given as follows by a gentleman of Boston: —

“After being about a month with us in Boston and its vicinity, and preaching every day, he went to Old York; preached there on Thursday, September 27; went on to Portsmouth, and preached there on Friday.
On Saturday morning he set out for Boston; but before he came to Newbury, where he had engaged to preach the next morning, he was pressed to preach along the way.
The house not being large enough to hold the people, he preached in an open field.
But having been infirm for several weeks, this so exhausted his strength that when he came to Newbury he could not get out of the ferryboat without the help of two men.
In the evening, however, he recovered his spirits, and appeared with his usual cheerfulness.
He went to his room at nine, his fixed time, from which no company could divert him, and slept better than he had for some weeks before.
He rose at four in the morning, September 30, and went into his private room; and his companion noticed that he was unusually long in private.
He left his private room, returned to his companion, threw himself on the bed, and lay there about ten minutes.
Then he fell on his knees and prayed most fervently to God that, if it was consistent with His will, he might that day finish his Master’s work.
He then asked his servant to call Mr. Parsons, the clergyman at whose house he was staying; but in a minute, before Mr. Parsons could reach him, he died, without a sigh or groan.
On the news of his death, six gentlemen set out for Newbury in order to bring his remains here: but he could not be moved; so his precious ashes must remain at Newbury.
Hundreds would have gone from this town to attend his funeral, had they not expected that he would be buried here....
May this stroke be sanctified to the Church of God in general, and to this province in particular!”
II. 1. We are, in the second place, to take some view of his character.

A little sketch of this was published soon afterward in the Boston Gazette; an extract of which is added here: — [“Little can be said of him but what every friend of vital Christianity who has sat under his ministry will attest.”]
“In his public labors he has, for many years, astonished the world with his eloquence and devotion.
With what divine pathos did he persuade the impenitent sinner to embrace the practice of piety and virtue!

[Filled with the spirit of grace, he] spoke from the heart, and, with a fervency of zeal perhaps unequaled since the days of the Apostles, [adorned the truths he delivered with the most graceful charms of rhetoric and oratory.]
In the pulpit he was unrivaled in his command of an ever-crowded audience.
Nor was he less agreeable and instructive in his private conversation: blessed with a remarkable ease of manner, willing to share, eager to edify.
May the rising generation catch a spark of that flame which shone with such distinguished luster in the spirit and practice of this faithful servant of the most high God!”
2. A more detailed, and equally just, account of his character has appeared in one of the English papers.
It may not be unwelcome to you if I add the substance of this as well: —
“The character of this truly pious person must be [deeply] impressed on the heart of every friend of vital religion.
In spite of a tender [and delicate] constitution, he continued, to the last day of his life, to preach with a frequency and fervor that seemed to exceed the natural strength of the most robust.

Being called to the exercise of his office at an age when most young men are only beginning to qualify themselves for it, he did not have time to make very considerable progress in the learned languages.
But this deficiency was amply made up for by a lively and fertile genius, by fervent zeal, and by a forceful and most persuasive delivery.

And though in the pulpit he often found it necessary to “persuade men” by “the terrors of the Lord,” he had nothing gloomy in his nature, being singularly cheerful, as well as charitable and tenderhearted.
He was as ready to relieve the bodily needs as the spiritual needs of those who came to him.
It ought also to be observed that he constantly urged every moral duty upon his hearers, particularly diligence in their various callings and obedience to their superiors.

He endeavored, by the most extraordinary efforts of preaching in different places, and even in the open fields, to rouse the lower classes of people from the utmost degree of inattention and ignorance to a sense of religion.
For this, and for his other labors, the name of GEORGE WHITEFIELD will long be remembered with esteem and veneration.”
3. That both these accounts are just and impartial will readily be granted; that is, as far as they go.
But they go little further than the outside of his character.
They show you the preacher, but not the man, the Christian, the saint of God.
May I be permitted to add a little on this subject, from a personal acquaintance of nearly forty years?
Indeed, I am fully aware how difficult it is to speak on so delicate a subject; what prudence is required to avoid both extremes, to say neither too little nor too much!
No, I know it is impossible to speak at all, to say either less or more, without incurring from some the former censure, and from others the latter.
Some will seriously think that too little is said; and others, that it is too much.
But without paying attention to this, I will speak just what I know, before Him to whom we must all give an account.
4. Mention has already been made of his unparalleled zeal, his tireless activity, his tenderheartedness toward the afflicted, and his charitableness toward the poor.
But should we not also mention his deep gratitude to all whom God had used as instruments of good to him? — of whom he did not cease to speak in the most respectful manner, even to his dying day.
Should we not mention that he had a heart capable of the most generous and the most tender friendship?
I have frequently thought that this, above all others, was the distinguishing part of his character.
How few have we known of so kind a temper, of such large and flowing affections!
Was it not chiefly by this that the hearts of others were so remarkably drawn and knit to him?
Can anything but love give birth to love?
This shone in his very face, and continually breathed in all his words, whether in public or in private.
Was it not this which, quick and penetrating as lightning, flew from heart to heart? which gave that life to his sermons, his conversations, his letters?
You are witnesses!
5. But away with the vile misconstruction of men of corrupt minds, who know of no love but what is earthly and sensual!
Let it be remembered, at the same time, that he was endowed with the most delicate and unblemished modesty.
His office called him to converse very frequently and at length with women as well as men; and those of every age and condition.
But his whole behavior toward them was a practical commentary on that advice of St. Paul to Timothy: “Appeal to the elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters, with all purity.”

6. Meanwhile, how suited to the friendliness of his spirit was the frankness and openness of his conversation! — although it was as far removed from rudeness on the one hand as from guile [and disguise] on the other.
Was not this frankness at once a fruit and a proof of his courage and fearlessness?

Armed with these, he did not fear the faces of men, but “used great plainness of speech” to persons of every rank and condition, high and low, rich and poor; endeavoring only “by the manifestation of the truth to commend himself to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”
7. Nor was he afraid of labor or pain, any more than of “what man [could] do to him”; being equally

blocks.x: Patient in bearing ill and in doing well.

s: And this appeared in the steadiness with which he pursued whatever he undertook for his Master’s sake.
Witness one instance for all — the Orphan House in Georgia, which he began and completed in spite of all discouragements.
Indeed, in whatever concerned himself he was pliant and flexible.
In such a case he was “easy to be entreated”; easy either to be convinced or to be persuaded.
But he was immovable in the things of God, or wherever his conscience was concerned.
None could persuade him, any more than frighten him, to depart in the least point from that integrity which was inseparable from his whole character, and which governed all his words and actions.
In this he did

blocks.x:
Stand like an iron pillar strong,
And steadfast as a wall of brass.

s: 8. If it is asked what was the foundation of this integrity, or of his sincerity, courage, patience, and every other valuable and lovely quality, it is easy to give the answer.

It was not the excellence of his natural temperament, not the strength of his understanding; it was not the force of education; no, nor the advice of his friends: it was nothing other than faith in a bleeding Lord; “faith of the operation of God.”
It was “a lively hope of an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that never fades away.”
It was “the love of God spread abroad in his heart by the Holy Spirit who was given to him,” filling his soul with tender, disinterested love for every child of man.
From this source arose that torrent of eloquence which frequently swept away all before it; from this came that astonishing force of persuasion which the most hardened sinners could not resist.
This it was which often made his “head as waters, and his eyes a fountain of tears.”

This it was which enabled him to pour out his soul in prayer in a manner peculiar to himself, with such fullness and ease united together, with such strength and variety both of thought and of expression.

9. I may close this point by observing what an honor it pleased God to put upon His faithful servant, by allowing him to declare His everlasting gospel in so many different countries, to such numbers of people, and with so great an effect on so many of their precious souls!
Have we read or heard of any person since the Apostles who testified to the gospel of the grace of God through so widely extended a space, through so large a part of the habitable world?
Have we read or heard of any person who called so many thousands, so many myriads, of sinners to repentance?
Above all, have we read or heard of any who has been a blessed instrument in His hand of bringing so many sinners from “darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God”?
It is true that, were we to talk this way to the fashionable world, we would be judged to speak like barbarians.
But you understand the language of the country to which you are going, and where our dear friend has gone a little before us.
III. But how shall we make good use of this solemn providence?
This is the third thing we have to consider.
And the answer to this important question is easy (may God write it in all our hearts!).
By keeping close to the grand doctrines which he delivered; and by drinking in his spirit.
1. And, first, let us keep close to the grand scriptural doctrines which he delivered everywhere.
There are many doctrines of a less essential nature about which even the sincere children of God (such is the present weakness of human understanding) are divided, and have been for many ages.
In these matters we may think and let others think; we may “agree to disagree.”
But meanwhile, let us hold fast the essentials of “the faith which was once delivered to the saints,” and which this champion of God so strongly insisted on, at all times and in all places!
2. His fundamental point was, “Give God all the glory for whatever is good in man”; and, “In the business of salvation, set Christ as high and man as low as possible.”
With this point he and his friends at Oxford, the original Methodists, so called, set out.
Their grand principle was: there is no power (by nature) and no merit in man.
They insisted that all power to think, speak, or act rightly is in and from the Spirit of Christ; and all merit is (not in man, however high in grace, but merely) in the blood of Christ.
So he and they taught: there is no power in man, until it is given him from above, to do one good work, to speak one good word, or to form one good desire.
For it is not enough to say that all men are sick with sin: no, we are all “dead in trespasses and sins.”
It follows that all the children of men are “by nature children of wrath.”
We are all “guilty before God,” liable to death, temporal and eternal.
3. And we are all helpless, with regard both to the power and to the guilt of sin.
“For who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean one?”
None less than the Almighty.
Who can raise those who are dead, spiritually dead in sin?
None but He who raised us from the dust of the earth.
But on what grounds will He do this?
“Not on account of works of righteousness that we have done.”
“The dead cannot praise You, O Lord”; nor can they do anything for the sake of which they should be raised to life.
Whatever God does, therefore, He does merely for the sake of His well-beloved Son: “He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities.”
He Himself “bore” all “our sins in His own body on the tree.”
He “was delivered up for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification.”
Here, then, is the sole meritorious cause of every blessing we do or can enjoy; in particular of our pardon and acceptance with God, of our full and free justification.
But by what means do we come to have a share in what Christ has done and suffered?
“Not by works, so that no man may boast”; but by faith alone.
“We conclude,” says the Apostle, “that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law.”
And “to as many as” thus “receive Him, He gives power to become the sons of God, even to those who believe in His name; who are born, not of the will of man, but of God.”
4. And “unless a man is” thus “born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
But all who are thus “born of the Spirit” have “the kingdom of God within them.”
Christ sets up His kingdom in their hearts: “righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.”
That “mind is in them which was in Christ Jesus,” enabling them to “walk as Christ also walked.”
His indwelling Spirit makes them both holy in heart and “holy in all manner of conduct.”
But still, since all this is a free gift, through the righteousness and blood of Christ, there is eternally the same reason to remember: “He that glories, let him glory in the Lord.”
5. You are not unaware that these are the fundamental doctrines which he insisted on everywhere.
And may they not be summed up, as it were, in two words — the new birth, and justification by faith?
Let us insist on these with all boldness, at all times and in all places — in public (those of us who are called to it), and at every opportunity in private.
Keep close to these good, old, unfashionable doctrines, however many contradict and blaspheme.
Go on, my brethren, in the “name of the Lord, and in the power of His might.”
With all care and diligence “keep safe that which is committed to your trust,” knowing that “heaven and earth will pass away, but this truth will not pass away.”
6. But will it be enough to keep close to his doctrines, however pure they are?
Is there not a point of still greater importance than this, namely, to drink in his spirit? — in this to be a follower of him, even as he was of Christ?
Without this, the purity of our doctrines would only increase our condemnation.
This, therefore, is the principal thing — to copy his spirit.
And granting that in some points we must be content to admire what we cannot imitate, yet in many others we may, through the same free grace, be partakers of the same blessing.

Conscious, then, of your own needs and of His bountiful love, who “gives liberally and does not upbraid,” cry to Him who works all in all for a measure of the same precious faith; of the same zeal and activity; the same tenderheartedness, charitableness, and heartfelt mercy.
Wrestle with God for some measure of the same grateful, friendly, affectionate temper; of the same openness, simplicity, and godly sincerity; “love without pretense.”
Wrestle on, until the power from on high works in you the same steady courage and patience; and above all, because it is the crown of all, the same unvarying integrity!
7. Is there any other fruit of the grace of God with which he was eminently endowed, and the lack of which among the children of God he frequently and passionately lamented?

There is one, that is, catholic love: that sincere and tender affection which is due to all those who, we have reason to believe, are children of God by faith; in other words, all those, in every denomination, who “fear God and work righteousness.”
He longed to see all who had “tasted of the good word” be of a true catholic spirit — a word little understood, and still less experienced, by many who have it frequently in their mouths.
Who is the one who answers to this description?
Who is the man of a catholic spirit?

One who loves as friends, as brethren in the Lord, as joint partakers of the present kingdom of heaven, and fellow heirs of His eternal kingdom, all, of whatever opinion, mode of worship, or congregation, who believe in the Lord Jesus; who love God and man; who, rejoicing to please God and fearing to offend Him, are careful to abstain from evil, and zealous for good works.

He is a man of a truly catholic spirit who bears all these continually on his heart; who, having an inexpressible tenderness for their persons and an earnest desire for their welfare, does not cease to commend them to God in prayer, as well as to plead their cause before men; who speaks comfortingly to them, and labors by all his words to strengthen their hands in God.
He assists them to the utmost of his power in all things, spiritual and temporal; he is ready to “spend and be spent” for them; yes, “to lay down his life for his brethren.”
8. How lovely a character this is!
How desirable to every child of God!
But why, then, is it so rarely found?
How is it that there are so few instances of it?
Indeed, supposing we have tasted the love of God, how can any of us rest until it is our own?
Why, there is a subtle device by which Satan persuades thousands that they may stop short of it and yet be guiltless.
It is well if many who are present here are not in this “snare of the devil, taken captive at his will.”
“Oh yes,” says one, “I have all this love for those I believe to be children of God; but I will never believe that anyone is a child of God who belongs to that vile congregation!
Can he, do you think, be a child of God who holds such detestable opinions? or he who joins in such senseless and superstitious, if not idolatrous, worship?”
So we can justify ourselves in one sin by adding a second to it!
We excuse the lack of love in ourselves by laying the blame on others!
To disguise our own devilish temper, we pronounce our brethren children of the devil!
Oh, beware of this! — and if you are already caught in the snare, escape out of it as soon as possible!

Go and learn that truly catholic love which “is not rash,” or hasty in judging; that love which “thinks no evil”; which “believes and hopes all things”; which makes all the allowances for others that we desire others to make for us!
Then we shall recognize the grace of God which is in every man, whatever his opinion or mode of worship: then all who fear God will be near and dear to us “in the tender affection of Jesus Christ.”
9. Was not this the spirit of our dear friend?
And why should it not be ours?
O You God of love, how long shall Your people be a byword among the heathen?
How long shall they laugh us to scorn, and say, “See how these Christians love one another!”
When will You roll away our reproach?
Shall the sword devour forever?
How long will it be before You bid Your people return from “following each other”?
Now, at least, “let all the people stand still, and pursue their brethren no more!”
But whatever others do, let all of us, my brethren, hear the voice of him who, being dead, still speaks!
Suppose you hear him say: “Now, at least, be followers of me as I was of Christ!
Let brother “no more lift up sword against brother, nor know war any more!”
Rather, put on, as the elect of God, heartfelt mercy, humility of mind, brotherly kindness, gentleness, long-suffering, bearing with one another in love.
Let the time past suffice for strife, envy, and contention; for biting and devouring one another.
Blessed be God that you have not long ago been consumed by one another!
From now on keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
10. O God, with You no word is impossible!
You do whatever pleases You!
Oh, that You would cause the mantle of Your prophet, whom You have taken up, now to fall upon us who remain!
“Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?”
Let his spirit rest upon these Your servants!
Show that You are the God who answers by fire!
Let the fire of Your love fall on every heart!
And because we love You, let us love one another with a “love stronger than death!”
Take away from us “all anger, and wrath, and bitterness; all clamor and evil speaking!”
Let Your Spirit so rest upon us that from this hour we may be “kind to each other, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, even as God, for Christ’s sake, has forgiven us!”
